Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Vignette:
Sione was fifty-one, a welder, his hands scarred from years of sparks and steel, and he had not driven a car in eight months. The crash had happened on a Tuesday evening, just after he’d finished a long shift at the fabrication shop. He was heading home, taking the familiar route past the old cannery, when a sedan ran a red light and slammed into the driver’s side of his pickup. The impact spun the truck into a utility pole. Sione remembered the screech of metal, the shatter of glass, and then the smell—sharp, sour, unmistakable—as the other driver staggered to his window, reeking of alcohol, asking if he was okay. Sione was not okay. His ribs were cracked, his left femur fractured, and he was pinned against the steering wheel, unable to move. For what felt like an eternity he hung there, half-conscious, the world tilting, the smell of beer and whiskey filling the cab.

The physical injuries healed slowly over months of physical therapy, but the memory of that evening did not. When the memory came—and it came without warning—Sione’s body would go rigid. He would feel his shoulders pressed back against an invisible seat, his legs locked in that same trapped angle, and the sharp, grinding pain would return to his ribs and thigh, even though the bones had long since mended. It was not just remembering; it was reliving—the shriek of metal, the flash of headlights, the sour stench of alcohol, all at once, so vivid that for a few terrible seconds he was back in the truck, waiting to die.

At work, the sounds of the shop became a minefield. A grinder hitting a steel beam, the clang of a dropped tool, the hiss of an air hose—each could send that full sensory wave crashing over him. He had learned to flinch, to freeze, to brace himself against the welding bench until the flashback passed. The other welders noticed; they started calling him jumpy, told him to relax. He could not explain. What frightened Sione most was that the memory seemed to own his body. He did not choose when it came, and while it lasted he was helpless.

He began to avoid anything that might trigger it. He stopped driving altogether—his wife, Leilani, drove him to and from work now, a forty-minute detour because she had to take back roads to avoid the intersection where it happened. He stopped going to the local bar where his old crew gathered after shifts; the first whiff of beer from someone’s glass had sent him into a full reenactment, his hands gripping the edge of the table, his breath short, his ribs aching. He told himself it was safer to stay home. But home was not safe either. A car accident on the evening news, the screech of brakes from the street outside, even the sound of Leilani opening a bottle of wine—each could trigger the same cascade of smells, sounds, and physical pain.

The consequences grew slowly. His supervisor pulled him aside and warned that if he kept freezing mid-task, he would be moved to inventory, a job with no welding, no future. His marriage grew quiet. Leilani would ask why he flinched when she hugged him from the driver’s side, why he couldn’t ride in her car without gripping the door handle. Sione could not put words to it. He only knew that the memory was still happening, as real as the day it occurred, and that he measured his life by the hours between flashbacks.

He finally agreed to seek help after Leilani said she could not keep driving him forever, that she was exhausted. In the therapist’s office, Sione sat stiffly, his hands on his knees, afraid to let his body relax. He was hoping, without quite believing, that someone could teach him to sit in a car without feeling the impact all over again. He was afraid that if he gave up the hyper-vigilance, the next time the memory came he would drown in it. But the weight of the avoidance had become heavier than the fear.
